new_statements.rule_in_words: Kunigami (Nakijin/Yonamine dialect) has no stress; it is a lexical pitch accent language built on quantity-sensitive iambic feet. Each morpheme carries at most one accent, on the penultimate mora (default) or final mora (marked); high pitch spans from a rise after the initial foot (or from the first mora) up to the rightmost accent, and the accent also blocks iambic lengthening of adjacent high vowels. Descriptively (Ogawa 2012:41; Sakimura 1984:19; Curry 2004:36) nouns fall into three surface classes: A = high from the 1st/2nd mora, B = high from the 3rd–5th mora (unmarked class), C = initial mora high followed by an obligatory fall.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated; feet are rhythmic units (iambic lengthening, aspiration foot-initial) but carry no stress.
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 9: 'This account is simplified. There are words with no accent, due to other factors. Unaccented words are pronounced with a High tone on the ultimate mora.' Ogawa 2012 and Lawrence 2013 note east/west Nakijin village pitch differences and variability in where the fall occurs; Lawrence (fall = accent) and Ogawa (rise = accent) disagree on which pitch event is contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical accent on simple words, cyclic assignment in compounds); Lawrence 2011 p.113 line refers to forms 'cited in isolation'; Nagano-Madsen 2014 shows phrase-level downstep across successive accents.
new_statements.identity_note: Every descriptive source found (both Glottolog refs and all downloaded papers) describes the Nakijin dialect, specifically the Yonamine (与那嶺) community of Nakijin-son on the Motobu peninsula, northern Okinawa Island. Glottolog places this under kuni1268 (Kunigami; sole dialect child Nago, nago1243); Pellard 2015 and Carlino 2022 doubt that 'Kunigami' is a valid subgroup and treat northern-Okinawan varieties as Okinawan. The statement therefore holds for Nakijin-Yonamine, not necessarily for Kunigami-son, Ie, Iheya or other northern-Okinawan dialects (Iheya has its own 2022/2026 chapters by Carlino).

sources.note: §3 p.115: Nakijin is 'a pitch accent language with an iambic foot structure. Stress plays no role in the phonology'; accents assigned cyclically to the penultimate mora (unmarked) or ultimate mora (marked); H tone on the rightmost accent and on the leftmost mora / first mora after the leftmost foot; quantity-sensitive iambic feet built left-to-right with iambic lengthening; aspiration is foot-initial, independent of accent; fn.9: some words are accentless and get H on the final mora; p.150-line: word-final H 'in forms cited in isolation'.

sources.note: p.1: the Yonamine/Nakijin dialect is unusual among Ryukyuan in having an accent in addition to tone (Lawrence 1990, 2001); the accent blocks lengthening of adjacent high vowels; H tone goes to the last accent and to the mora after the initial foot; verbs: accent on the pre-final mora of the ending /-iuN/, position predictable from word structure.

sources.note: §2 pp.51–52: Ryukyuan accent types are (i) falling-kernel (Shuri, fixed on the 2nd mora), (ii) rising-kernel where the place of the pitch rise is distinctive, exemplified by Nakijin, (iii) accentless (Irabu); repeats Ogawa's three types; F0 study shows the Nakijin HL 'falling' type differs from Tokyo-type falls and that sequences of rising accents use downstep.

sources.note: p.41 (1) 今帰仁方言の3型アクセント: A型 = high pitch from the 1st or 2nd mora; B型 = high pitch from the 3rd–5th mora; C型 = word-initial mora high with an obligatory fall right after; B is the unmarked, C the most marked type; the prosodic unit is the mora and the contrastive element is the rise (昇り核); foot structure is essential (Rhythmic Lengthening).
